utterances.text: We made a request to the command of the 2nd Corps to have the seals made, and when the seals had been made we handed them over to Mr. Hasan Muratovic in Dzevanica [phoen]. He was supposed to deliver the seals to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was your information about whether he had ever done that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't even know anything about that until we received another document telling us that the seals had not arrived, and that we should send them again somehow, and that we should go to the command of the 2nd Corps and have them do it and we did that in March. We found the documents that had not been delivered. We handed them over to the command of the 2nd Corps, and I don't know to this day whether those seals ever arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say March, what year are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know if and when Naser Oric arrived in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Oric arrived in Tuzla in March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did they have stamps in Srebrenica in 1992 to 1994, the sort of stamps that they were requesting, stamps and seals?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sure they didn't. There wasn't even a place where seals could be made, where stamps could be made. They couldn't even make them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In your system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from your experience working in unions and in other capacities, would it be permissible for someone just to make stamps and start using them or do you need some sort of authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law, both before and after the law [as interpreted], a stamp could be made only if there was a court decision, and pursuant to that, a seal could be made. It could not be made under any other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to have to move ahead. Do you know Ferid Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he ever come to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in 1993 he arrived in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he explain what the situation had been like in his area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I saw and met Ferid Hodzic was when he arrived from Srebrenica, and in Lucavik [phoen] a meeting was held, attended by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. The meeting was attended by other heads of municipalities of the Tuzla district, including us, from Bratunac, Vlasenica and Srebrenica municipality, who were headquartered in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what did he say about the situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you put this question. I had noticed Ms. Richardson standing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do regret having to make this objection at this point in time in light of the fact that we are short on time. However, this information that's being elicited from this witness is going outside the summary that we were provided. This is a very important individual whose name we've heard time and time again, and I think it would have been best if the Defence would have notified us yesterday that this witness was prepared to talk about meetings held with this individual who had been in Srebrenica. And at this point, Your Honour, I think this is hampering the Prosecution from conducting a proper examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson. Do you have any further questions for the witness on this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply what Ferid Hodzic said about the situation in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Srebrenica. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he describe what the situation was like in the whole region, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. In detail. He described the situation of chaos where there was a shortage of food, medicines, health care, weapons, clothing, footwear and everything else. It was a situation of chaos, and he left for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I won't pursue in light of Ms. Richardson's objections, but I think this is not evidence which we haven't heard before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move ahead, but I would suggest that you do exactly as you suggested now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I have two -- well, one last exhibit, D859.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This concerns an interview allegedly, an interview with General Sead Delic. It's entitled Oric left Srebrenica on his own accord. I simply want to go to page 2 of 5 where having been asked a question, General Delic said the following: "I can only state my opinion. Brigade commanders were not in that group. As far as I know, Naser came on his own accord. No one had invited him. I know for sure that late Ejub Golic, a commander of a battalion, also came with them. He died in the breakthrough through the Serb lines, in order to have his responsibility for several murders in Srebrenica established. I know his case very well. The commander Rasim Delic charged me with deciding whether to send him back or try him here, since there was substantial evidence that he had been implicated in several murders in Srebrenica. Discussed this for a long time and finally decided that his potential crimes do not fall under the statute of limitations, that he would be held responsible for them sooner or later and that the priority at that time was to send him back to Srebrenica." I simply have two questions. Do you know anything about what's described there firstly, about Ejub Golic being returned to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ejub Golic came to Tuzla, and he was interviewed in the command of the 2nd Corps. But later on, when we attended a meeting attended by Mr. Sead Delic, he ordered that Mr. Golic go to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think I just have time or one or two more questions. This might seem like a strange question, but you described how you were in Tuzla during the war. Do you know who in December 1992 was eating in the canteen in Srebrenica, if indeed there was a canteen?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if Rambo was there, he could have gone from Srebrenica to Tuzla whenever he liked and brought the mail with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Well, it was, you've told us how dangerous it was to return to -- to go to Srebrenica. Did in fact your father die trying to go back to Srebrenica from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was so anxious to get to Srebrenica. My late father, in his great desire to reach Srebrenica, was killed on the way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No further questions? You've finished or for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think my -- I thought my time was up, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less it is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, please. I'm just going to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would have given you an extra four or five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that case, I do have an exhibit which actually I would be grateful. I thought that my time was up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then do it now, please, so that Ms. Richardson can start with her cross after you have finished completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, if the witness could be shown D300, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As you can see from the top of this it refers to a tape recording of a session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on 11 August 1995. If we turn to page 4 of the English, we see the president, Alija Izetbegovic, and this is dealing, as you can see, it's after the fall of Srebrenica, and we see President Izetbegovic saying: "Clear answers should be given to these questions because they are constantly repeated. The commander of the division was not inside at the time of the attack. He was taken out for two months. Of course people are asking why he did not come back meanwhile," et cetera. And it says: "We must have an answer to this and a clear one, no matter what that is." And then we see Delic and this -- I don't believe it's in contention but this is actually a different Delic, Rasim Delic, at page 5, and we see the following: "We did what we could. Now it turns out that command and control do not function in this unit. They chose the commander. They said you're going to be an intelligence operative as of tomorrow. The thing is that they are still at the year 1992 level." Now, my question is: You've referred to information you heard about what was happening in Srebrenica from people who were evacuated, from people who came from Srebrenica. Does what is stated there correspond at all to what you learned from them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We turn a bit further to -- it's the last paragraph at page 7 firstly. And it's Delic and they say talking about Naser Horic firstly, as if they don't in fact know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there is a correction which I need to make in the English actually, Your Honour, between the English and the B/C/S. In the English it says, talking about Naser Horic, President Naser Horic did not - I repeat this here at the Presidency meeting and the president knows this personally - he did not ask to return by helicopter. In B/C/S it's he asked to return by helicopter. It's a small point but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's important to point out, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we see on the next page, page 8 in English, referring to Naser Horic, or Oric: "However, my information now, when he came here and when the army came, he did not have much influence on his brigade as commander. He was not a commander who had command over the situation in the division. He had command over his own brigade and another one. He had no influence over the others. So the level of military organisation in this area was low. We tried to bring as much influence to bear as we could in writing by orders and summoning all commanders. Regretfully it did not work."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the same question. You've mentioned meetings which you attended. Does this reflect what you heard about the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what was said at the meeting which took place immediately after the fall of Srebrenica in the building of the Tuzla canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who else was present at that meeting, the one that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others, there was the president, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic; the commander, Mr. Rasim Delic; Mr. Sead Delic of the 2nd Corps; Mr. Salih Malkic, the Chief of Staff of the Tuzla CSB; Mr. Hazim Rancic; Mr. Izet Hadzic, the president of the then canton. It was already the Tuzla canton. Many mayors of neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. And we will have a 30-minute break. That means we'll start at ten to 4.00 -- 5.00. Ten to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's start. Before we start, just wanted to confirm that since there was a query from your side, whether we were authorising the defence to reply to your response and whether there would be a right for a rejoinder, the answer is yes to both. They are authorised to reply to your response and you are authorised to file a rejoinder. The same applies to the Rule 92. You've asked whether you could reply to that. Yes, please go ahead. In fact, my opinion, although I haven't consulted Judge Brydensholt on it, that we would rather concentrate more on the Rule 92 issue for the time being to know exactly where you stand, and there will be some recommendations to you by our Senior Legal Officer in the meeting on Thursday without, of course, prejudice to the whole matter. It's a suggestion that I asked him to make, along the lines that we adopted in Brdjanin, generally speaking. It was a system that we adopted with exceptions here and exceptions there obviously because we all remained as flexible as we could. But it's just an idea. You will talk about it with Mr. Von Hebel on Thursday. All right? But you have, of course, our authorisation to file replies and rejoinders and so on and so forth. Ms. Richardson. You've got until tomorrow morning and if you need more, even later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, did you say I have until tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, my name is Joanne Richardson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have -- we plan to finish at 6.30, maximum --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the caveat that if I am stopped at any time by the gentleman in particular, of course, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And my calculation is that the Prosecution have until 6.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We finish not she has the right to go on until 6.35. She has one hour, 25 minutes, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and then re-examination by us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mustafic, I apologise for all of the discussion prior to beginning your cross-examination about time but time is a concern, as you've heard, and so I do have a series of questions for you, seeking to clarify your testimony, and in addition, I will be asking you some questions about your familiarity with various individuals from Potocari and Srebrenica. First off, you were shown a document, and that is Defence Exhibit 300, the very last document, and perhaps the usher could assist me by putting this document before the witness. Now, my first question to you is whether or not you'd seen this document prior to your testimony here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I take it you've not had an opportunity to read through this document prior to it being put to you a few minutes ago by Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I would direct you to page -- page 5 of the English. I believe it's page 4 of the B/C/S, and please correct me if you can't find it. I'm referring you back to the exact same area that you were asked a series of questions about. And first off, I would ask you to confirm that Mr. Oric was not present at this meeting, that is -- that has been memorialised by this document. As far as you know, he wasn't present?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Presidency meeting? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Right. And this Presidency meeting, in fact, occurred after the fall of Srebrenica. In fact, it's dated on the 11th of August 1995. If you look at the first page. I apologise I have you going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the fall of Srebrenica occurred in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the fall of Srebrenica was particularly important to the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Especially the Presidency in Sarajevo and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And if you would turn as I asked you before to page 4 of the B/C/S, and there is a discussion that occurs prior to what Mr. Delic is being quoted as saying, in fact it may be paraphrasing what he's saying. But there is a reference to Potocari, and if you would look to the section and I would just read the first sentence -- well, it begins, if you find the word "UNPROFOR," I will start with that particular -- just before that. "Perhaps even during the night" --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give him a chance to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the reference in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe it's on page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said page 4 initially in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Maybe I'm mistaken, but it's ERN 01824955. And it's the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you see that? Okay. Now there is a discussion. Is that -- Mr. Mustafic, can you follow? Okay. Now, there is a discussion taking place here --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And perhaps I should say that it follows the -- appears to follow the president's remarks from page 4. And it says here: "Then I went on that trip the next day," he's obviously speaking about information that he had received from someone who had been to Srebrenica. "I went on that trip the next day. We were at the assembly when it was reported sometime after noon that the strike had just happened, but then they reported that UNPROFOR had withdrawn to Potocari then after noon that the Serbs were entering Potocari," et cetera. Now, based on your reading of this portion of this document, would you agree that this information is in reference to the events which occurred in 1995 and not events relating to 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dating from 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, this portion which follows Mr. Delic's name, it says: "We did what we could. Now it turns out that command and control did not function in this unit." Do you have any idea what unit they are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the 8th Operations Group or the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And following that, it says: "They chose the commander. They said you're going to be -- you're going to be an intelligent operative as of tomorrow. The thing is they are still at the year 1992 level." Now, having heard or read the rest of this statement, do you agree that this person, Mr. Delic, is not referring to events that occurred in 1992 or 1993, but, in fact, he is discussing the events relating to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It clearly says here that the men said that they were practically at the 1992 level, and he's referring to the entire organisation up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are referring to the general situation of chaos, that nothing was functioning, the command and control system, nobody obeyed nobody else and that this was the very reason why Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Right. But they are referring to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995. Would you agree with me that that's what this report and that's what these comments relate to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took place after the fall of Srebrenica. It was in that context that they discussed the fall of Srebrenica. But in this portion, where Mr. Delic spoke, they referred to the situation as it was from the very beginning, that it was a situation of chaos. Nobody knew what the others were doing and that the same thing happened in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But that's not what it says here. That's your own assessment of what's being presented here. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My own assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand -- you understand now why I said go ahead to Mr. Jones earlier on when you objected on the basis that it would be pure speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you for that reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk to you about your -- some of the individuals from the Potocari area. I believe you said that you were born in Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you went to school there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So I take it you would be very familiar with most of the people from that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And prior to -- to -- I'll withdraw the question and rephrase it. Have you heard -- had you heard of Naser Oric prior to going to Tuzla in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were born and bred in the same area, in the area of Potocari, I knew him very early on in my childhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you knew that he had been a former police -- that he had been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what was Naser Oric's role in Srebrenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're asking him as regards prior to his departure on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to leaving for Tuzla in April of 1992, what role, if any, did Naser Oric play with respect to what was happening in the area? And I say with respect to what was happening, meaning the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1992, the war had not yet started there. Whatever was going on was the same as in any other place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in the Podrinje area where we lived. To put it simply, people were frightened, they did not know what was going to happen. Nothing was organised in that period, and nobody knew anything and the people were simply waiting for things to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. You will have to keep your answers brief. If you don't know, just say you don't know. If you need more time to answer, I think that that will not be a problem. But for now, if you could just answer my question. So as far as you know, prior to your leaving, Naser Oric did not playfully role with respect to the conflict in April of 1992? A simple yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, once you arrived in Tuzla, did you hear anything about Naser Oric in the area of Srebrenica, and when I say "hear anything," I mean did you hear anything with respect to any type of role he played in organising the people of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated that I was unable to hear anything about it because the telephone lines were down. I was even unable to make contact with my own family. Therefore, I couldn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard any type of information coming out about what was going on in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard something was when a group arrived from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in late October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did this group mention or did you hear either from this group or anyone else, that Naser Oric had organised a resistance in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no organised resistance in the area of Srebrenica. Rather, in some parts, wherever people lived, they would get organised, groups of them, in an attempt to defend themselves from the aggression. In other words, they were defending their own families and properties. Mr. Oric was in the area of Potocari. He was with a group of lads there putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you hear that he was the leader of this group in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Together -- he was together with others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you hear if there was a leader of the group?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was a group of people there who got organised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is important. The interpreters didn't catch up the entire answer. What I have here on the screen is you said, you answered, "I said that there was a group of people there who got organised." And then you said something else, but the interpreters didn't catch the rest of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said there was nobody appointed leader of the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is this what you learned, that actually -- someone actually told you, Mr. Mustafic, there was no one leading the group in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From conversations with those who arrived from there, I learned that there was a group of lads there and that nobody was singled out of them as the leader of the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness says and what hasn't been entered clearly in the transcript is that nobody mentioned any leaders of the groups. I believe that's what the witness should clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has clarified it now. I think he has clarified it now. Yes, go ahead Ms. Richardson. Thank you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did anyone mention -- I'll rephrase that question. Did you learn that Srebrenica in May of 1992 had been liberated by Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not receiving almost any information. Whatever information we had we received or, rather, we obtained whilst listening to the Serb media, since there was a media blockade in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you didn't learn anything about what was going on in Srebrenica until October of 1992? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered you, but if you want to repeat your question, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, let's go to October of 1992. Is that the first time that you had direct communication with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how was it that you were able to communicate with them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through amateur -- through radio amateurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So prior to October of 1992, you were not aware that individuals in Srebrenica had been using the amateur radio station to contact family members in Tuzla and the wider area of Srebrenica -- excuse me, of Sarajevo and even outside the country?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Where was your office located in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located at Rudarska Street in Tuzla at number 51.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is that the Tuzla -- in the town, the area of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you learn prior to October of 1992, via the Serb radio or anyone else, that Srebrenica had organised a territorial staff, a Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't learn that there was a meeting in May 1992, where Naser Oric was named a commander of the territorial staff of Srebrenica? Territorial Defence, excuse me, of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you know nothing of the other groups that had organised, that were organised in the Srebrenica area, headed by Hakija Meholjic or Akif Ustic or Zulfo Tursunovic? Were you aware that there were other groups that had been organised?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know anything during that period, because there was a full blockade in place. The only thing we could hear was through the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, the reason that I'm asking you these questions is so that when you say you don't know anything, it's important for us to establish what the anything you're referring to is so that the information that you are giving us will assist us. So I take it you were not aware that Ramiz -- someone by the name of Ramiz Becirevic had also been a member of the Territorial Defence staff of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't know anything about Srebrenica, about the setting up of any sort of staff there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that the fighters in the area of Srebrenica, or the men who were subordinated to Naser Oric, had been engaging in combat actions in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that only through the Serb media, radio and television.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So at some point you did hear that Naser Oric was the commander of the Srebrenica forces, and that they were involved in combat action in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had only heard that from the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think I can anticipate what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's just that in all the previous questions there's no time period being mentioned. The witness is clearly stating that what he heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree entirely with you. Perhaps, Ms. Richardson, you can re-address the matter to the witness and I think a simple question would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did you actually hear from time to time on the Serbian radio and at what time frame was this? I mean what time period was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard over the Serb media that units or, rather, Muslim forces were attacking Serb villages around Srebrenica. This was in the time period of September, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And did these radio reports or Serbian media reports mention specifically Naser Oric? If they did, did they specify what role he played and whether he was involved in these attacks? And last question -- I'm trying to help you and to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last part would be: Were any of these Serbian villages or villages that were supposedly attacked by the Muslim fighters mentioned? Let's take them one by one. Were the Serbian villages mentioned or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Some Serb villages around Srebrenica were mentioned. As far as mentioning any names, I said that they mostly used expressions such as Turks, Ustashas were attacking and so on and so forth. So they did not specify any names, be it first or second names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do I take it from you that over the Serbian radio the name of Naser Oric was never mentioned in connection with these alleged Muslim attacks?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: From what he heard obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I heard, no. Tuzla had no electricity for quite a while, so we were not able to listen to the radio or watch television, that is, any newscasts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in October of 1992, when you were able to make contact with Srebrenica, what if anything -- who did you make contact with? Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone in particular basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, anyone in particular.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention my mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, just taking you back again to when you -- from the time you left Srebrenica in April to October of 1992, did you learn anything about Srebrenica establishing a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When was the first time you learned that Srebrenica established a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received the letter that was brought over to me by the lads from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, prior to that letter being brought over, had you already established an office to represent Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And under whose authority did you establish this office?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the authority and the laws of the Tuzla district.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you register with Tuzla in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were registered as an association of displaced persons and refugees with the registration court in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But were you registered as representing Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no. We were only registered as an association of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so the first time you actually represented Tuzla -- excuse me, Srebrenica, was when you received a letter from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I represented the interests of the Srebrenica people even earlier on. Of all those people from Srebrenica who happened to be within the Tuzla district at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood his testimony on examination-in-chief. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just that he had said that he was only registered as representing Srebrenica on a certain date but that he was representing Srebrenica and its interests before then. So it was in my submission a misconstruction of what he had said to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember exactly what he had said on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When did you -- when were you given an office to -- from where you can work, from where you and the other representatives could work?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we established the association of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When was this? What time period?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many of you -- I believe you said that it was yourself and two other individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The association of refugees was an organisation gathering all the displaced persons and refugees from the area of Srebrenica. I and two other people were mentioned in the letter that we received from Srebrenica that we could represent them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you testified before that you could not communicate with Tuzla -- excuse me, with Srebrenica before October of 1992. And could you tell us how it is that the people in Srebrenica knew to contact yourself and the other individuals to represent them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps if you can straight away tell him what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will understand for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You said you received the letter in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: From the War Presidency in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Authorising you to represent the War Presidency. My question is: If you could not communicate with them, with Srebrenica, as you've testified, how is it that the War Presidency in Srebrenica knew to send a letter to you about representing them? How did they learn of you or about you? Why did they contact you versus anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, they did not make contact with me. They knew I had gone to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But they knew you had gone to Tuzla in April; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when one could leave the area for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I take it you were not the only person who left the area for Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So my question is: Why did they contact you in particular and not anyone else? Did they learn that you had been working on behalf of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate they did not make contact with me, but sent an authorisation to me in a letter. Before the war, I was a businessman and I was a representative of the Srebrenica municipality trade union organisation. I had good organisational skills, and I believe that was the reason why my name was in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine. Now, at some point, the -- your organisation grew, and that is from yourself and two other individuals. Did you later on have more people working in your office as representatives for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many people did you have working for you between -- working with you as part of the Tuzla office in 1992 up until 1995, July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that office, in the association of refugees, there were about 15 people who were involved and active in order to somehow supply those people with humanitarian aid, meaning food, clothes, footwear and accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as part of your function, that being a humanitarian effort on their behalf, how many refugees would you say you worked with or worked on behalf of from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 3.000 to three and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And part of your function, I take it -- well, I'll rephrase the question. Was all of the 3.000 people that you were working on behalf of, were they all entitled to receive benefits such as accommodation, food, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But the objective circumstances and the area of the free territory of the canton were such that many were not able to have a roof over their heads. That's why they were put up in various schools, in Mejdan and other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you worked with the Tuzla authorities to assist them with finding housing, food, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to cooperate with the Tuzla authorities because we were on their territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it that you at some point, after -- well, I'll rephrase the question. The families that you worked with, the refugees, were they also family members of the fighters or the soldiers from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they were families from Srebrenica municipality. The families of all those who had remained in Srebrenica and been unable to get out for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand that. But my question is: Were they also families of individuals who stayed in Srebrenica and had been there fighting or defending Srebrenica? When I say Srebrenica, I mean the entire area, the wider area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, your organisation -- I believe you said you had about 15 people working between -- from the time you started in 1992 up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the beginning, from 1992 to 1993. Staffs were abolished and then when the War Presidency representative office was registered, I think we had some 18 people doing that job.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In 1994, would you say you had more than 18 people? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact number. If I were to list their names, I might be able to enumerate them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me assist you by showing you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance. This is a new document and it is DA18-3721. While that's being handed out, I will read the title. It says "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica, War Presidency, Tuzla Committee, 16 February 1994." And it's by War Presidency, Srebrenica Municipality, Tuzla Committee, Mirsad Mustafic, economist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafic, could you take a look at this document, and I would ask you if you recall preparing this document on behalf of your -- the Srebrenica municipal office in Tuzla? I should say it lists yourself and 27 or, I should say 26, it numbers a number of individuals, your name is listed as number 1, to 27. Do you recall that? And this document describes the task and the duties of all of the individuals at the office. Would that be -- does this ring a bell? Is this familiar to you? You have to say yes --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And now is it your testimony that all of these individuals listed here had been working on behalf of the refugees from the Srebrenica office?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just for the record, and please tell me if you agree, that you had drivers, you had someone who worked on the finances. It says, number 8, for instance, Fazlic, SF, worked object on general issues; number 16, Mr. Gadzo, worked on logistics, et cetera. So this would be -- if you could confirm that this is some of the tasks that the members of your office engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Ms. Richardson. What's the next number, please? P...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P600, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which has reference number DA18-3721, consisting of one page in B/C/S and three pages in English, being entered as a Prosecution Exhibit marked as P600.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just so that we can understand the document better, you sent this to the president of the Srebrenica Municipal Assembly, and the purpose that it was sent to the Srebrenica was so that they could give their consent or approve the lists that you provided to them, including yourself, that you were engaging in working on behalf of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because -- go ahead. I only have the first page in B/C/S, but it seems that it's -- it has a second page which I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my record entry is not correct. It contains two pages in B/C/S and not one page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. And in fact if we could have -- if I could have the usher's assistance in giving this document back to the witness so that he can see the second page. If there is no second page, then I will provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please provide it later. Let's not waste time but please provide it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So he can read from my copy and we'll provide a full set.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafic, I do apologise, but there is a second page. Now, the remarks on the second page, it says that: "We ask you for the sake of the uninterrupted work of the committee to immediately give consent to the proposed list of military conscripts who have worked on the above-mentioned positions from the very first day of -- very first day the committee was formed and send that consent to the district people's defence staff, municipal people defence staff, Tuzla, 2nd Corps command." So my question to you is could you just confirm that you sent this list to Srebrenica so that this would prevent the 2nd Corps from mobilising you and the other individuals? Would that be a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One point of curiosity, why are all the family names or the surnames which end in "ic" with a double C? Is that correct or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist, I myself asked this question. It appears that based on the typeset of the computer, that it replaces the diacritics, the [indiscernible], yes. I myself was curious, so I did find out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not at all. It's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I see that all the time it's double C, double C, double C.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's the language, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mustafic, moving right along, I have another document that I would ask to be placed before you. And this is DA18-3483. It's a new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. In the meantime, I could continue, Your Honour, and we will find the copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, in your dealings with Tuzla and in your contact with them to assist you with helping the Srebrenica refugees, did you receive financial support from them by way of money to help the families of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Tuzla, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you never received any financial support from Tuzla by way of money?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you receive any -- did you have contact with Mr. Hazim Sadic about the refugee -- about your work on behalf of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Hazim Sadic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if I could have the document placed before you, this is a document, I'll read the title, army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 2nd Corps command, hope I'm not talking too fast, Tuzla, 3rd of February, 1994, and it's to the command of the 8th Operational Group in Srebrenica, and it is signed by Hazim Sadic. Now, you testified that you are familiar with Mr. Sadic and you worked with him in Tuzla in your capacity as a representative for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before? If you could just briefly just take a quick look at it, it discusses a number of matters --?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could he answer that question first, please. It's important to the question. Has he seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] if he could look at it while he's describing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question has been asked and he hasn't answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him look at it first because it's a rather longish document and deals with more than one thing. And then you ask him whatever you like. When you have finished reading it, Mr. Mustafic, please tell me so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Are you done, Mr. Mustafic? I see you looking up.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is the first time you've seen this letter that was sent from Mr. Sabic [phoen] to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now I'd just like to verify or ask you a couple of questions about the contents of this document. I'll just read from the first paragraph, beginning with the sentence -- well, I'll read from the beginning. In your first document, 3294, dated the 1st of February, 1994, you requested the answer to your document 6791/93 dated 11 of November, 1993 in which you ask for help in food and accommodations for 608 soldiers and their families from your area. Now, further on it says: "Without investigating the background and the motives of this request, we are informing you that we sent the answer in the document 11/1297 dated 26 of November, 1993 to the commander Naser Oric on the measures taken not only for those families but also for others for whom you urgently requested." Now my question to you is, at least with respect to this -- first of all, were you aware that they had received a request, Mr. Sabic had received a request from Naser Oric regarding measures on behalf of families?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to -- I'll go a bit further down. "In your document number 697-1/93 dated 11th November, 1993 you sent us a list of 608 soldiers and their families with requests to help them financially and in accommodation within our possibilities." Now, I would turn to the second page that begins with the paragraph "2nd corps command," and without reading through the entire portion of this document, there is a mention of money being given for the families. And it says that a cash advance for July and August 1993. And further down it states on the same day, again a portion of money was paid for 702 families of killed and 343 for families of heavily wounded soldiers. And further down, the second paragraph, this is where you're mentioned, it says: "Your committee in Tuzla was notified of these activities, and they are in possession of the list of families and soldiers having this right and they have received the instruction on how to distribute this money and other, and they only had to visit the family to give them the money." And further down your name is mentioned. "From the sent list of 608 names, the majority of people probably has that right, the list was sent by Mirsad Mustafic who had the responsibility to inform us on everything that has been done." My question to you is: Does this information here sound familiar, that a list was provided to the Tuzla authorities containing 600 names, of the 608 names of fighters and their families, of soldiers and their families, and also there is a reference to an amount paid for 702 families of killed and 343 for families of heavily wounded soldiers. Does this information sound familiar to you with respect to what your organisation was doing in cooperation with Tuzla and assisting the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But may I explain in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, I would prefer that -- that's -- I just need a confirmation, and I fear that I'm running out of time, so perhaps Mr. Jones may want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I even dispense Mr. Jones from his intervention. Let him explain. But please be as brief as possible. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very briefly, in connection with funds, in 1993 helicopters were used to transport the wounded from Srebrenica to Tuzla. They were accommodated in hospitals and clinics in Tuzla. When they left the hospitals, we were forced to find them accommodation. After that, in view of the fact that Tuzla had certain legal regulations in place, we started an initiative to create an association to assist disabled fighters and to deal with this kind of work. However, we had to prove everything. We had to prove that they were disabled. We had to have lists. And this list was drawn up by the service of the Disabled Fighters' Protection Association, based on medical opinions from doctors, and then they received certain financial assistance from the government, which, as you see, was given out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it that in order to receive assistance, you -- one had to at least establish where it was that you served in the military, when you served, and I take it this type of information was important to establishing to -- for the person to acquire financial support?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were proceedings with witnesses to prove this. There were retroactive things that took place, just so that people would get assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just an objection to a double question. It's always dangerous when there are two questions about whether you had to something in the military and then whether that was important. It's two separate questions, and there is always a danger that the answer will be a misunderstood. But also, since Ms. Richardson has been using the word "soldiers," which I see in the translation, it's [B/C/S spoken] in the original and the witness has been saying fighters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that observation which I am sure Ms. Richardson will take note of. Yes, yes, but it's probably the translation, the wrong translation on the document in any case. Yes, let's move ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you also receive information from Srebrenica corroborating the involvement of particular fighters so that either they or their families could receive financial assistance in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In a certain period of time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. So did you ever receive information from Srebrenica which confirmed or gave information that soldiers or fighters or individuals had participated in various attacks, or when they were -- when they became a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And at no time did anyone in Srebrenica contact you on behalf of any of the families of fighters from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They contacted me only for me to visit certain families in certain areas and help them with accommodation, food and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were these families families of fighters? Including families of fighters, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were families that were on the territory of Tuzla municipality, of everyone who was there, including fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have a P number for this document DA18-3483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Richardson. This document, which consists of two pages in Serbo-Croat and three pages in English, with reference number DA18-38 -- 3483, being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P601.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would ask the usher's assistance in handing up a new document. And in the interests of time, I will read the title heading from the document. Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica Municipal Assembly, War Presidency Committee in Tuzla. And it is dated the 23rd of June, 1995. It is apparently sent to RP department of combat issues Srebrenica. And it is by Mirsad Mustafic, president.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafic, could you take a look at this document. And I would ask if you've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, does this confirm what you previously testified to, about the fact that an organisation or at least it was necessary to establish disabled combats and so that they would be able to receive benefits as a result?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could give a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, to cut it short, this will be P602. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just so that, while you still have the document before you. The bottom of the document has an additional sentence or two. One sentence, actually. It appears that there is a note Ibrahim Becirevic, and it says the stations Kenwood, TS 850, serial number, a donation of Muhamed Ikanovic, to Sead and Senad Dubasic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you -- were you sending this information to Mr. Becirevic about communication equipment donated? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can -- I'm not sure, did you already assign a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I take it that you were not the only individual in the office preparing documents? I think we've seen a document that was prepared by another representative in your office.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would ask the usher's assistance with a new document, and that is DA17-1494.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is army of ABiH, command of 8 Operational Group Srebrenica, Srebrenica classified 03-125, and it is dated the 7th of February, 1995. And it is to Srebrenica Municipality Committee based in Tuzla, attention Mirsad Mustafic, and it is signed by Naser Oric, commander, Brigadier. Now, Mr. Mustafic, do you recall receiving this document from Naser Oric? If you could just take a look at it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, this document is being entered and marked as P603.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the information in the document, do you recall giving information on a Mr. Tihic, Daut -- obviously I'm not pronouncing his name correctly. How is his first name pronounced?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you don't recall giving or receiving or requesting information about this individual?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not request or receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it states that Mr. Tihic is a member of the armed forces of the Biljeg TO, on the 8th of May, 1992. It states where he performed his duty, and also it states that he's no longer an ABiH soldier. Do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where is he from?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the territory of the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It says here that he's from Lijesce?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lijesce, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is that in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, he was in Srebrenica during 1992 and up until 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came with the wounded from Srebrenica in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is the type of information that one would give if one was seeking to obtain financial assistance as a disabled soldier, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. What is incorrect about what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't see this document or write it. And as for the facts that the document is addressed to Mustafic, well, all the documents were actually addressed personally to Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Is what you're telling us is that some documents you just never saw and is this being addressed to you or is there another -- you can answer my first question. Did you see all of the documents coming into your office that were addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. But my question is: I understand that you've never seen this document being sent to you. My question is: Is this the type of information that one would give if you're seeking to get disability as a disabled soldier and financial assistance, accommodation for your family, et cetera? Would they give information of when you joined the military and where you were based in addition to the unit, et cetera? This is important information, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a bit earlier that as far as -- that we proceeded in such a manner that we would try to find eye-witnesses in Tuzla, then there would be an administrative procedure and we would be proving these matters retroactively. As for this particular document, I've never seen it, I never requested or received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand. Now, from what you know of Mr. Tihic, would you estimate that he was born in 1962? Would that be the correct date of birth, from what you recall, his age?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew Tihic only superficially. I don't know when he was born or where he is, his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to -- the witness to be shown Prosecution's Exhibit 571, and we do have copies. Pardon me. We have a copy, Your Honour, for the ELMO. I apologise. It was not put on the list previously but it's very...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We do need to see it since we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I mean, we too. I didn't even know it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can put the English on the ELMO, which is being done by the usher as we speak, and the witness can have -- the particular page that I will be referring the witness to actually is number 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we cannot proceed this way. Our client is entitled to see the document, to see what it is about, and we are also entitled to have the document in the original. And our client in particular has the right to have a copy of it because he passes on instructions to us in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, if I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Time is running short for you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you've got more important matters to address, I would suggest you move to more important matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the only thing I can say at this point is that I'd ask that judicial notice be taken that number 44 on the list is Mr. Tihic, on this list, that P571, and I think we can move on from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I mean, I don't think you need the witness to confirm that. If he's on the list, he's on the list. If he isn't, he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, so I know how much time I have, it's 6.35?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. 6.35 we walk out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 6.22 because she had one hour, 25 minutes, and we started at 4.57. I'm recalculating everything, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So if you could give me the exact time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, because I thought we had a note here that says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only if there is the indulgence of Mr. Jones who --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, I certainly hope Mr. Jones will indulge us. It's only --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I need to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ten minutes at least at this point, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Richardson, and try to restrict yourself to what is really important.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The next document, Your Honour, is -- it's a new document. It's 04118030 to 8031.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, just in the interests of time, this document is entitled Army of BiH Republic, command of the 8 Operational Group Srebrenica, Committee of Srebrenica Municipality in Tuzla, and it is sent to Mr. Mirsad Mustafic. The relevant portion it's -- that I will read -- I'll just wait for a moment so the witness can have the document before him. This is a certificate and it involves Mr. Nirzad Karamujic, born in Bratunac, resided in Burak [phoen], has been a member of the ABiH since the 6th of August, 1992, and that he's a winner of the Golden Lily. And it is signed commander, 280 IBLB, Potocari, Major Ibrahim Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mandic, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour, Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mandic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, I would --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafic, do you recall this information being sent to you by Mr. Mandic from Srebrenica or from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the second -- the document deals with two persons, Mr. Mustafic. It's not the first one, who is Bektic Arif, but it's the second, the second certificate, which refers to Mirsad Karamujic, son of Ahmo. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall this information being sent to you, the certificate being sent to you, by Mr. Mandic regarding Mr. Karamujic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUSTAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular certificate, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have a P number, and I will be asking the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Exhibit P604.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I will be distributing ERN number 03425951 and 03425949, which is the B/C/S, and perhaps we can take notice, judicial notice, of the fact that Mr. Karamujic is mentioned here in this document as having received the Golden Lily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know about judicial notice, Your Honour. If it's merely a submission, that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is a submission. Basically we can look at the documents and we don't need to take judicial notice of it. If it's there, it's there. If it's not, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this series of questions, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the relevance is that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you trying to prove actually?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have put documents before other witnesses regarding proposed commendations, and the Defence has always asserted that none of the individuals either proposed or out of Srebrenica had received any commendations or awards, and that is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a mischaracterisation of our position. We never took such an extreme position, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, based on the questions that have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's -- so these are two documents or one document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's one document, one is in English, the translation, and it's from a book, it's from the same book, monograph, Golden Lily, are BiH army members decorated in 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these two pages in B/C/S, two pages in English together are being entered as P605. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document, it's DA17-7404. And also document ERN 02115198.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, in the interests of time again I will read, Army of the BiH Republic and of the 8 Operational Group Srebrenica. It's dated 18th of January, 1995, Srebrenica Municipality Committee in Tuzla, and it's attention Mirsad Mustafic and it is signed by Naser Oric. Mr. Mustafic, as you look at this document, do you recall receiving information from Naser Oric about Mr. Enes Ibrahimovic, who was born in Sapotnik and who was a member of the 284th East Bosnia Light Brigade performing the duty of assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training. The document goes on to list additional information about his military service. And I'm also handing up ERN 02115198, and this is -- the document is entitled the 284 East Bosnia Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to the second document, Your Honour, it just confirms or just, I should say, has the name Ibrahim Ibrahimovic of the 284 command, brigade command, and his name is listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
